name: North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice
description: Master the North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice with detailed grip mechanics, transition steps, and finishing pressure. Complete BJJ submission guide.
summary: The North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice is a high-percentage blood choke that threads the choking arm under the neck during the transition out of crushing jaw pressure, compressing both carotid arteries with a gable grip and hip sprawl.
overview:
The North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice leverages the intense jaw pressure already established in the Shoulder of Justice position to seamlessly transition into one of the highest-percentage blood chokes in grappling. Unlike entering the North-South Choke from standard side control or north-south, this variation uses the opponent's compromised defensive structure—head turned away, near arm trapped, posture broken by sustained pressure—to thread the choking arm under the neck before the defender recognizes the threat.

The setup begins with the cross-face arm sliding from shoulder pressure into an underhook beneath the opponent's neck while the attacker walks their hips toward the head. The transition itself maintains constant pressure, preventing the critical window where defenders typically insert frames or recover head position. Once the gable grip locks and the hips sprawl past the opponent's head, the choke compresses both carotid arteries through the combined mechanics of arm squeeze, chest-to-shoulder pressure, and hip sprawl.

This submission chain is particularly effective because the Shoulder of Justice creates a dilemma: endure the jaw pressure or react defensively. Both options feed directly into the North-South Choke entry, making it a natural complement to the pressure-based control strategy that defines the Shoulder of Justice position.

injury_risks.injury: Carotid artery compression leading to loss of consciousness
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential for longer-term effects if held after unconsciousness

injury_risks.injury: Tracheal compression and windpipe damage from misaligned grip
Cervical spine stress from improper release or forced neck positioning
injury_risks.recovery_time: Weeks to months depending on severity

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from explosive bridging attempts under choke pressure

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum to allow partner to recognize the danger and tap before full compression
tap_signals: Multiple rapid hand taps on opponent's body
Multiple rapid foot taps on the mat
Any distress signal including body convulsions or going limp
Loss of resistance indicating possible unconsciousness
release_protocol: Immediately release arm pressure and unlock gable grip upon any tap signal
Roll off opponent's head and neck area completely without jerking their neck
Allow opponent to recover in side-lying position with airway clear
Monitor for signs of consciousness and normal breathing patterns
If opponent is unconscious, place in recovery position and alert medical staff immediately
training_restrictions: Never apply explosive or jerking pressure to the neck during the choke transition
Always ensure partner has clear tap access with at least one hand throughout the sequence
Never hold the choke after partner taps or goes limp under any circumstances
Beginners should practice only the positional transition and grip placement without applying choking pressure
Never use competition speed or full pressure in training—apply progressively and give time to tap

variations_and_setups.description: Thread the cross-face arm from Shoulder of Justice shoulder pressure beneath the opponent's neck, walk hips toward the head, lock a palm-to-palm gable grip at the jaw line, and sprawl to finish. This is the highest-percentage entry when the opponent's head is fully turned and near arm is controlled.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent's head is turned away from jaw pressure and near arm is trapped or controlled

variations_and_setups.description: When the opponent's near arm ends up between your choking arm and their neck during the threading phase, include the arm in the choke rather than fighting to remove it. The trapped arm adds compression against the neck and reduces their ability to frame. Adjust grip position slightly higher to account for the arm bulk.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent's near arm is caught inside the choking grip during transition and cannot be cleared

variations_and_setups.description: Before initiating the arm thread, secure a far-side underhook to control the opponent's far arm and eliminate their primary frame defense. This removes the biggest obstacle to completing the choke but requires momentarily releasing some shoulder pressure to reach the underhook. Best used against opponents who consistently frame with their far arm.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against opponents who consistently insert far-arm frames during the choke transition

attacker.name: North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to execute the North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice. Step-by-step guide covering grip transition, hip positioning, and finishing mechanics.
attacker.overview: Executing the North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice requires precise timing of the grip transition from cross-face shoulder pressure to neck encirclement. The attacker must maintain constant pressure throughout the transition to prevent the defender from recognizing the shift and inserting defensive frames. The key advantage of this entry is that the Shoulder of Justice has already broken the opponent's defensive posture, turned their head, and restricted their near arm, creating ideal conditions for threading the choking arm beneath the neck. Success depends on smooth, incremental hip walking toward the north-south angle combined with progressive arm deepening around the neck before committing to the gable grip lock and finishing sprawl.
key_principles: Maintain constant chest-to-body pressure during the entire grip transition from shoulder pressure to neck encirclement
Walk hips toward the head in small incremental steps rather than one large movement that alerts the defender
Thread the choking arm deep beneath the neck past the trachea before committing to the gable grip lock
Lock the gable grip tight against your own chest at the jaw line to maximize bilateral carotid compression
Sprawl hips completely past the opponent's head and drop chest weight onto their shoulder line before squeezing
Squeeze elbows together using chest and back muscles rather than pulling with arms to generate sustainable choking pressure
setup_requirements: Established Shoulder of Justice position with sustained jaw pressure turning opponent's head away
Opponent's near arm controlled or trapped to prevent frame insertion during the threading phase
Stable base with hips connected to opponent's hip line and far knee posted wide for balance
Cross-face arm positioned at the shoulder-neck junction ready to transition from pressure to underhook
Opponent's defensive structure compromised by sustained pressure with head turned and posture broken

execution_steps.description: Verify your Shoulder of Justice is fully established with shoulder blade driven into the opponent's jaw at a 45-degree angle toward their far shoulder. Hips must be heavy on their near hip line with near arm controlled or pinned. Confirm your base is stable with far knee posted wide before initiating the choke transition. Do not begin the threading if your position is not consolidated.

While maintaining chest-to-body contact and downward pressure, begin sliding your cross-face arm from the static shoulder pressure position to thread it beneath the opponent's neck. Use the angle created by their turned head as the entry path for your forearm. This movement must be gradual and disguised within your normal pressure adjustments to avoid alerting the defender to the grip change.

Take small incremental steps with your hips toward the opponent's head, shifting your weight progressively from a side-control angle toward the north-south angle. Each step should deepen your arm position around the neck while keeping your chest heavy on their torso. Do not lift your hips or create any gap between your body and theirs during this walk—every step maintains or increases pressure.

Once your threading arm has passed sufficiently around the neck and past the trachea, bring your free hand to meet it and secure a palm-to-palm gable grip pulled tight against your own chest. The grip should sit at the base of the opponent's jaw near their ear where the carotid arteries are most superficial. Avoid gripping too low on the neck where compression targets the trachea rather than the arteries.

Sprawl your hips past the opponent's head while dropping your chest weight onto their shoulder line. Your body should arrive perpendicular to theirs with your head positioned near their far hip. Maintain the gable grip tight to your chest throughout the entire sprawl movement to prevent any gap between your arm and their neck that would relieve arterial compression.

Drive your elbows together toward each other while simultaneously dropping your shoulder weight downward and extending your hip sprawl further. The choke compresses both carotid arteries through the combined mechanics of arm squeeze, chest-to-shoulder pressure, and hip extension. Increase pressure progressively and smoothly over three to five seconds, giving your training partner time to recognize the choke and tap.

If the initial squeeze does not produce a tap within several seconds, make micro-adjustments without releasing any pressure. Walk your hips slightly to change the compression angle, tighten the grip closer to the jaw line where arteries are more accessible, or increase your sprawl to drive more body weight through the choking arms. Small positional adjustments often produce significant changes in choke effectiveness without requiring a full reset.

common_counters.counter: Frame insertion with forearms before grip locks
common_counters.your_response: If opponent gets forearms between their neck and your threading arm, abandon the choke attempt and re-establish Shoulder of Justice pressure to reset. Re-apply jaw pressure to break their composure, then reattempt when they make a different defensive reaction.

common_counters.counter: Bridge and turn toward the choking arm
common_counters.your_response: Ride the bridge by widening your base and dropping hips heavier. Use their turning momentum to accelerate your hip walk toward north-south. Their turn often deepens your arm position rather than creating escape space.

common_counters.counter: Hip escape away creating distance during transition
common_counters.your_response: Follow their hip escape with your own hip movement, maintaining grip contact. If they create significant distance, transition to standard north-south control and attempt the choke from there. If grip is lost, return to side control and re-establish Shoulder of Justice.

common_counters.counter: Pushing your head away with both hands to create space
common_counters.your_response: Their hands on your head means their arms are extended and vulnerable. Maintain your threading arm position and use chest pressure to collapse their arm structure. Both arms on your head also means zero frame defense against the choke itself.

common_errors.error: Lifting shoulder pressure during the arm threading transition
common_errors.consequence: Creates space for the defender to insert frames, reposition their head, and recognize the choke setup, killing the attack before it begins
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant chest-to-body contact throughout the entire grip change by sliding the arm while keeping your torso weight on the opponent

common_errors.error: Threading the arm too shallow around the neck
common_errors.consequence: Produces a trachea choke rather than a blood choke, which is slower, more painful, gives more escape time, and is less effective against determined opponents
common_errors.correction: Drive the forearm deep under the neck past the Adam's apple to position at the jaw line where carotid arteries are most superficial before locking the gable grip

common_errors.error: Rushing the hip walk with large movements
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recognizes the transition, inserts frames during the pressure gap, and the choke attempt fails with a return to neutral side control
common_errors.correction: Walk hips in small incremental steps maintaining pressure at each position, disguising the transition within normal positional adjustments

common_errors.error: Locking the gable grip too low on the neck away from the jaw line
common_errors.consequence: Reduces compression on the carotid arteries and creates a windpipe choke that opponents can endure longer while working escape sequences
common_errors.correction: Position the grip at the base of the jaw near the ear where arteries are most superficial, using the jaw line as your anatomical landmark

common_errors.error: Pulling with arms rather than squeezing elbows together
common_errors.consequence: Rapid arm fatigue from using biceps rather than chest muscles, plus inconsistent compression that allows blood flow past the choking surfaces
common_errors.correction: Squeeze elbows together using chest and back muscles while driving body weight downward through the arms for sustainable, bilateral compression

common_errors.error: Failing to sprawl hips completely past the opponent's head before squeezing
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient downward pressure through the choking arms, and opponent can use your body position to create bridging leverage for escape
common_errors.correction: Complete the full north-south hip sprawl with your head near their far hip before committing to the finishing squeeze

common_errors.error: Attempting the choke without first controlling the near arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent frames with their near arm during the threading phase, blocking the arm from circling the neck and forcing an abort
common_errors.correction: Ensure the near arm is trapped under your body weight or controlled before initiating the arm threading transition

training_progressions.focus: Arm threading path and grip placement
training_progressions.description: Drill the arm threading from Shoulder of Justice cross-face to neck encirclement with zero resistance. Partner lies still while you practice sliding the arm beneath the neck, finding the jaw-line grip position, and locking the gable grip. Focus on maintaining chest contact throughout. Repeat 20 times per side.

training_progressions.focus: Coordinating hip movement with arm deepening
training_progressions.description: Add the hip walk toward north-south while threading the grip. Practice the coordinated movement of stepping hips toward the head while simultaneously deepening the arm around the neck. Partner remains passive but provides feedback on pressure gaps felt during the transition.

training_progressions.focus: Gable grip lock, sprawl mechanics, and squeeze technique
training_progressions.description: From an already-established North-South Choke position with grip locked, practice the sprawl and elbow squeeze finishing mechanics. Partner provides feedback on choke tightness and compression location. Focus on using body weight and elbow squeeze rather than arm pulling.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 4: Full Chain with Progressive Resistance
training_progressions.description: Execute the entire Shoulder of Justice to North-South Choke sequence against a partner providing 50-75% resistance. Partner attempts realistic defenses including frame insertion, bridging, and hip escape. Attacker must recognize defensive reactions and either adjust or reset to Shoulder of Justice.

Timed rounds starting from Shoulder of Justice with full resistance. Practice deciding when to commit to the choke versus abandoning and returning to pressure control. Include transitions to alternative submissions when the choke is defended.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the North-South Choke primarily compress to produce unconsciousness?
flashcards.answer: The North-South Choke primarily compresses both carotid arteries on the lateral sides of the neck, restricting blood flow to the brain. The choking arm encircles the neck and the combined squeeze of the arms, chest pressure, and hip sprawl creates bilateral compression. This is a blood choke that produces unconsciousness in approximately eight to twelve seconds under full compression, making prompt release upon tap absolutely critical.

flashcards.question: Your opponent inserts a forearm frame during your arm threading—what is the correct response?
flashcards.answer: Do not force the choke against an established frame. Release the threading attempt, re-establish Shoulder of Justice pressure with your shoulder driven back into their jaw, and reset completely. The frame indicates they recognized the transition early. Re-apply sustained jaw pressure to break their defensive composure, then reattempt the choke when they react to the pressure with a different defensive movement that exposes the neck.

flashcards.question: What makes entering the North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice different from entering from standard north-south position?
flashcards.answer: The Shoulder of Justice entry provides three significant advantages. First, the opponent's head is already turned away by sustained jaw pressure, creating a clear path for the threading arm. Second, the near arm is typically trapped or controlled, preventing frame insertion. Third, the opponent's defensive structure is already compromised by the relentless pressure, reducing their reaction time and available defensive options during the grip transition.

flashcards.question: Why must you squeeze elbows together rather than pulling with your arms when finishing this choke?
flashcards.answer: Pulling with your arms engages the biceps and forearm flexors, which fatigue rapidly and produce inconsistent compression against the neck. Squeezing your elbows together toward each other activates the larger muscles of the chest and back, creating sustainable force that compresses both sides of the neck symmetrically. Additionally, the elbow squeeze maintains structural integrity of the gable grip, while pulling loosens the grip and allows the opponent to create space between your arm and their neck.

flashcards.question: What are the immediate signs that you should release the choke during training?
flashcards.answer: Release the choke immediately upon any tap signal including verbal submission, hand taps on your body, or foot taps on the mat. Release immediately if the opponent goes limp, stops resisting entirely, or shows involuntary movements such as body convulsions. In training, always err on the side of early release. If there is any doubt whether your partner tapped, release and ask rather than holding and waiting for a clearer signal.

flashcards.question: Where should the gable grip sit relative to the opponent's jaw for maximum arterial compression?
flashcards.answer: The gable grip should sit at the base of the opponent's jaw near the ear, where the carotid arteries pass closest to the skin surface. Gripping too low on the neck targets the trachea rather than the arteries, producing a slower airway choke that gives more escape time. Gripping too high near the chin misses the arterial targets entirely. The jaw line serves as the primary anatomical landmark for optimal grip placement and maximum blood choke effectiveness.

trap: Slide grip down to the chest

flashcards.question: Why is rushing the hip walk toward north-south a critical error during setup?
flashcards.answer: Rushing the hip walk creates two significant problems. First, large movements lift your chest pressure off the opponent's body, opening space for frame insertion and head repositioning that prevents the choke from being established. Second, large movements are far easier for the defender to recognize and react to than small incremental steps. The defender feels the sudden weight shift and immediately inserts defensive frames. Small steps maintain constant pressure and disguise the transition within normal positional adjustments.

flashcards.question: In competition, when should you commit to finishing versus abandoning the choke and returning to Shoulder of Justice?
flashcards.answer: Commit to the finishing squeeze when your gable grip is locked at the jaw line and your hips have completely cleared past the opponent's head into the north-south position. If you have not secured a solid grip or your hips are still in transition, the choke is not yet viable and you should return to Shoulder of Justice pressure control. Maintaining the dominant positional control is more valuable than gambling on a low-percentage choke attempt with an incomplete setup.

trap: Commit as soon as threading starts

flashcards.question: How should you release the North-South Choke safely after your partner taps?
flashcards.answer: Upon any tap signal, immediately unlock your gable grip and remove your arms from around the opponent's neck without any jerking motion. Roll your body off their head and neck area completely to eliminate all compression. Allow your partner to recover in a side-lying position with their airway clear and do not manipulate their neck in any direction. If they appear disoriented or were briefly unconscious, place them in the recovery position and monitor their breathing until they are fully alert.

plausible: Let go but stay on top

defender.name: North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice Defender
defender.description: Defend against the North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice. Recognition cues, frame insertion timing, and escape strategies for BJJ practitioners.
defender.overview: Defending the North-South Choke from Shoulder of Justice requires recognizing the transition from pure jaw pressure to choke setup before the gable grip locks around your neck. The critical defensive window occurs during the arm threading phase—once the grip is secured and hips sprawl past your head, escape becomes extremely difficult and tapping is the safest option. Early recognition of the weight shift and arm movement pattern allows you to insert forearm frames, recover head position, or create the hip distance needed to prevent grip completion. Understanding the attacker's sequential steps gives you clear intervention points where defense is most effective.
key_principles: Recognize the grip transition early—the moment shoulder pressure shifts to arm threading is your highest-percentage defensive window
Insert compact forearm frames against the threading arm before it passes under your neck to block the choke path
Fight the grip before it locks—once the gable grip is secure, escape probability drops dramatically and tapping becomes the safe choice
Create hip distance through well-timed shrimping when the attacker commits weight toward your head during the transition
Keep elbows tight to your body to create structural barriers that prevent the arm from sliding deep under your neck
Turn your chin toward the choking arm side to compress the space available for arm threading
recognition_cues: Shoulder pressure shifts from static jaw compression to a sliding movement along the side of your neck toward an underhook
Opponent begins walking their hips toward your head in small incremental steps rather than maintaining hip-to-hip connection
The cross-face arm starts threading and circling beneath your neck rather than maintaining static downward shoulder pressure
Weight distribution noticeably shifts from your hip line toward your head and shoulder area
Opponent's free hand reaches toward the threading arm to establish a grip connection around your neck

defensive_options.action: Insert forearm frame against the threading arm to block neck encirclement
defensive_options.when_to_use: As soon as you feel the cross-face arm sliding from static pressure to threading under your neck—this is the highest-percentage window
defensive_options.if_successful: Blocks the choke setup completely and forces attacker to return to Shoulder of Justice pressure position
defensive_options.risk: If frame is too late and arm is already deep, you may trap your own arm inside the choke

defensive_options.action: Chin tuck and turn toward the choking arm side to compress threading space
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the arm has begun threading but the gable grip is not yet locked—turning your chin blocks the arm path
defensive_options.if_successful: Prevents the arm from deepening around the neck and stalls the choke attempt at an incomplete stage
defensive_options.risk: Turning toward the attacker can expose your back if they abandon the choke and transition to back control

defensive_options.action: Hip escape away during the attacker's weight shift toward your head
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker commits weight toward your head for the north-south transition and their hip pressure on your hip line lightens
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates enough distance to recover guard position before the choke can be completed
defensive_options.risk: If timing is off, the hip escape can accelerate the attacker's transition to north-south rather than creating escape distance

defensive_options.action: Bridge and roll toward the choking arm side when grip is partially set
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has begun the hip walk but grip is not yet locked—use as a scramble initiator
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the attacker's base and positioning, forcing a reset to side control or creating a scramble
defensive_options.risk: If the bridge fails, you have expended significant energy and the attacker can re-establish position with better control

escape_paths: Insert forearm frames during the arm threading phase and hip escape to recover half guard or closed guard before the gable grip locks
Turn chin toward the choking arm to compress the threading space, then shrimp away to create distance for guard recovery
Bridge explosively during the hip walk transition to disrupt the attacker's base and create a scramble back to neutral position

favorable_outcomes.how: Insert frames during the arm threading phase when the attacker transitions from Shoulder of Justice pressure, then shrimp aggressively to recover closed guard before the gable grip can be established

Block the choke attempt early with forearm frames or chin positioning, forcing the attacker to abandon the choke and return to Shoulder of Justice pressure where you can continue working standard side control escapes

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to react to the grip transition from shoulder pressure to neck threading
common_errors.consequence: Once the gable grip locks and hips sprawl past the head, escape success drops below fifteen percent and the choke reaches full compression within seconds
common_errors.correction: React immediately when you feel the shoulder pressure shift from static jaw compression to a sliding arm movement—this is your highest-percentage defensive window

common_errors.error: Pushing against the attacker's body with fully extended arms
common_errors.consequence: Extended arms are vulnerable to kimura attacks and provide no structural resistance against the threading arm circling the neck
common_errors.correction: Use compact forearm frames positioned close to your neck rather than extended arms, creating structural barriers through bone alignment without exposing your limbs

common_errors.error: Panicking and making explosive random movements when the choke begins to tighten
common_errors.consequence: Burns energy rapidly while creating openings that help the attacker settle into a tighter finishing position—the choke tightens on uncontrolled movement
common_errors.correction: Stay calm and focus on systematic frame insertion and hip escape rather than explosive bursts that accelerate your fatigue and improve the attacker's position

common_errors.error: Trapping your own arm inside the choke by reaching across your body to fight the grip
common_errors.consequence: Your trapped arm adds compression against your own neck, making the choke tighter and removing your ability to create defensive frames
common_errors.correction: Keep your arms on the outside of the attacker's choking arm, never reaching between the arm and your own neck where your limb becomes a choking tool against you

flashcards.question: How do you recognize the North-South Choke setup from Shoulder of Justice before the grip locks?
flashcards.answer: The key recognition cues are a shift in shoulder pressure from static jaw compression to a sliding movement along the side of your neck, the attacker walking their hips toward your head in small incremental steps, and their cross-face arm beginning to thread under your neck rather than maintaining static downward pressure. The weight distribution also shifts noticeably from your hip line toward your head and shoulder area. Any of these cues should trigger immediate defensive action.

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to signal submission when caught in this choke?
flashcards.answer: Tap clearly and repeatedly on the attacker's body with your hand, or verbally submit loudly if your hands are restricted. Multiple rapid taps are easier for your partner to feel than a single tap. If both hands are restricted, tap rapidly with your feet on the mat. Do not wait until the choke is fully locked to tap—the North-South Choke can produce unconsciousness within seconds of full bilateral compression, so tap as soon as you recognize the grip is locked and you cannot escape.

plausible: Wait until the grip is set
trap: Grit it out and don't submit

flashcards.question: What defensive options are available and at what stage of the attack should each be employed?
flashcards.answer: Frame insertion against the threading arm is your highest-percentage defense and should be used the moment you feel the arm sliding under your neck during the initial transition. Chin tuck and turning toward the choking arm is your secondary option if the arm has begun threading but the gable grip is not yet secured. Hip escape during the attacker's weight shift is your tertiary option for creating distance during the transition phase. After the gable grip locks, your best option is to tap immediately.

flashcards.question: Why is panicking and making explosive movements particularly dangerous when defending this choke?
flashcards.answer: Explosive uncontrolled movements burn energy rapidly while creating openings that actually help the attacker settle into a tighter finishing position. The North-South Choke mechanically tightens on movement because thrashing creates gaps that the attacker fills with deeper arm positioning and heavier sprawl pressure. Calm, technical defense focused on frame insertion and timed hip escape is far more effective than explosive bursts that accelerate your fatigue and improve the attacker's finishing position.

flashcards.question: What is the consequence of waiting too long to begin your defense against this choke?
flashcards.answer: If you wait until the gable grip is fully locked and the attacker's hips have sprawled past your head, escape success drops dramatically even for advanced practitioners. At this stage, bilateral carotid compression is established and increasing, leaving you only seconds before blood flow restriction produces unconsciousness. The critical defensive window is during the arm threading phase—once that window closes, tapping immediately is the safest option rather than risking consciousness loss from a fully locked blood choke.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the transition from pressure to choke setup
training_progressions.description: Partner transitions slowly from Shoulder of Justice to North-South Choke at quarter speed. Practice identifying each recognition cue—arm sliding, hip walking, weight shifting—and calling out the transition verbally before taking any defensive action. Build pattern recognition before adding physical defense.

training_progressions.focus: Placing defensive frames during the arm threading window
training_progressions.description: Partner performs the arm threading at half speed. Practice inserting compact forearm frames against the threading arm at the correct timing—after the arm begins sliding but before it passes under the neck. Focus on frame placement precision and structural integrity rather than strength.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Integrated Defense with Hip Escape
training_progressions.focus: Combining recognition, framing, and hip escape into a complete defensive sequence
training_progressions.description: Partner performs the full Shoulder of Justice to North-South Choke transition at 50-75% speed and resistance. Practice the complete defensive chain: recognize the cue, insert the frame, then hip escape to recover guard. Reset when defense succeeds or choke locks. Increase partner speed progressively.

training_progressions.focus: Defensive composure and decision-making under realistic conditions
training_progressions.description: Full resistance positional sparring starting from Shoulder of Justice. Partner attempts the North-South Choke at realistic speed and pressure. Practice maintaining composure, recognizing the setup under duress, and choosing the appropriate defensive response. Tap early when the grip locks to build safe training habits.
